Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture *Ion channels and membrane potential*. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

---

**Q1.** A membrane protein moves 500 molecules of glucose per second. Another moves 10 million K⁺ ions per second. Which is a channel and which is a transporter? Give one more property that tells them apart.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Does the protein change shape for every molecule, or is it an open pore?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The glucose mover is a **transporter** (10²–10⁴ per second: it binds, changes shape and releases each molecule). The K⁺ mover is a **channel** (up to 10⁸ ions per second through an open pore). Other differences: a transporter is **never open to both sides at once** and can be coupled to ATP or another gradient to move a solute **uphill**; a channel only lets ions flow **down** their electrochemical gradient.
:::

---

**Q2.** Na⁺ is smaller than K⁺. Why can it not pass through the K⁺ channel's selectivity filter?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does an ion have to lose before it enters the narrow filter, and what does the filter give back?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
To enter the narrow filter, an ion must lose its **shell of water**, which costs energy. For K⁺, the filter's **backbone carbonyl oxygens** sit at the same distance as the water oxygens did, so the cost is paid back. Na⁺ is smaller; the rigid filter cannot close in on it, so the oxygens are too far away to replace its water. Losing water without being paid back costs too much, so Na⁺ stays out.
:::

---

**Q3.** Match each channel to how it is opened: (a) voltage-gated Na⁺ channel, (b) nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, (c) Piezo2. Gating types: ligand, mechanical force, voltage.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One has a charged sensor helix, one binds a transmitter, one responds to stretch of the membrane.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(a) **voltage**: positive charges in a sensor helix move when the membrane depolarises. (b) **ligand**: two acetylcholine molecules bind and open the pore. (c) **mechanical force**: membrane tension pulls on its blades; Piezo2 senses touch.
:::

---

**Q4.** Use the Nernst equation ($E = \frac{61.5\text{ mV}}{z}\log_{10}\frac{c_\text{out}}{c_\text{in}}$ at 37 °C) to calculate $E_\text{K}$ if K⁺ is 150 mM inside and 15 mM outside.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The ratio out/in is 0.1. What is log₁₀(0.1)?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$E_\text{K} = 61.5 \times \log_{10}(15/150) = 61.5 \times (-1) =$ **−61.5 mV**. A tenfold gradient of a singly charged ion gives about 61.5 mV. The sign is negative because K⁺ is higher inside: the inside must be negative to hold K⁺ back.
:::

---

**Q5.** The resting membrane potential of a cell is −70 mV, $E_\text{K}$ is −89 mV and $E_\text{Na}$ is +67 mV. Why is the resting potential so much closer to $E_\text{K}$ than to $E_\text{Na}$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which channels are open at rest?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
At rest, many **K⁺ leak channels** are open and very few Na⁺ channels. The membrane potential is a weighted average of the equilibrium potentials, weighted by permeability (the Goldman idea). K⁺ dominates, so the potential lies near $E_\text{K}$, pulled a little towards $E_\text{Na}$ by the small Na⁺ leak.
:::

---

**Q6.** During an action potential, why does the voltage fall again after the peak, and why can a second action potential not start immediately?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Two things happen to two kinds of voltage-gated channels after the peak.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The voltage-gated **Na⁺ channels inactivate** (a part of the channel plugs the pore from inside), and slower voltage-gated **K⁺ channels open**, so K⁺ flows out and the voltage falls towards $E_\text{K}$. Inactivated Na⁺ channels cannot reopen until the membrane has been negative for a short time: the **refractory period**. This also makes the signal travel in only one direction along an axon.
:::

**Q7.** In a cell-attached patch-clamp recording, the current jumps between 0 and −2 pA and never stays in between. What does this tell you, and about how many ions per second pass through the channel when it is open? (Charge of one ion: 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
1 A = 1 C/s. Divide the current by the charge of one ion.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The square steps show **one channel** switching between **fully open and fully closed**; there is no half-open state. 2 × 10⁻¹² C/s ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C ≈ **1.25 × 10⁷**, about **12 million ions per second** through one protein molecule.
:::

---

**Q8.** Two patients have cystic fibrosis. Patient A is homozygous for G551D, patient B for F508del. Ivacaftor alone helps A a lot but B very little. Explain.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where is the CFTR protein in each patient, and what does a potentiator do?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**G551D** CFTR reaches the plasma membrane but its **gate rarely opens**. Ivacaftor is a **potentiator**: it increases the time the channel is open, so it fixes this defect. **F508del** CFTR **misfolds in the ER** and is degraded, so almost none reaches the surface; a potentiator has nothing to act on. Patient B needs **correctors** (elexacaftor, tezacaftor) to help the protein fold and reach the membrane, plus the potentiator, because rescued F508del also gates poorly.
:::
